title: Generative tools and embedded AI: Firefly

opening.headline: We examine Adobe Firefly's terms of use and source information to determine whether images created with AI can be used in business documents or whether the use of AI must be disclosed.
body: There are times when you want to include images created by AI in advertising drafts or presentation materials. At this point, two questions arise. Can I use this image for work or commercial purposes, and do I have to disclose that it was created with AI?

In this class, we will first distinguish between creation tools that create images, videos, and voices and the built-in AI contained in documents or design tools. Next, read Adobe Firefly's frequently asked questions about terms of use, training data, and attribution information, and list items to look for in ad draft cases.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain image, video, and voice creation tools and AI built into business tools
Distinguish between the terms of use of the product and the need for disclosure

screens.title: The image I created, should I use it or reveal it?
screens.lead: I am trying to use a generated image in an advertisement design. Read below and think about what questions you need to ask.

visual.alt: On the left is a mock-up of the advertisement, and on the right is a scene with a speech bubble saying that this image was created by AI.

paragraphs: I am planning to use an image created by AI as the background for a new product advertisement design. It's very convenient because you can describe the mood you want in a sentence and an image will appear within a few minutes.

However, you cannot tell just by looking at the image whether this image can be used commercially in advertising or whether you need to disclose to readers or customers that it was created with AI. The answer lies in the terms of use established by the tool, the regulations of the organization, and the standards of the medium.
Today we will look at how to find and read the terms of use and disclosure sections in the documentation provided by the tool.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Are something that is easy to make and something that can be used the same thing? At the end of the lesson, you will be able to answer this question with a checklist.

screens.outro: First, let me recall my experience using AI images in my work.

screens.title: Experience writing AI images
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever used AI-generated images in your work documents?
items.answer: It is often used as an illustration for presentation materials or as a cover image for a proposal. There is less burden for internal data, but if the data is disclosed externally or used commercially, there are more things to check.

items.prompt: Did you check the terms of use then?
items.answer: In most cases, it was written without checking. Terms of use may vary for each tool and function, so even for tools from the same company, terms may vary depending on the function. In this class, we will specifically identify where to read.

items.prompt: Are you using the AI functions in word processors or design apps in the same way?
items.answer: The AI built into the app is convenient because it can be used right away while working, but the terms of use are subject to the terms set by the tool. The first step is to think separately between standalone creation tools and embedded AI.

screens.outro: Let’s start by distinguishing between generative tools and embedded AI.

screens.title: Built-in AI for creation and business tools
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how AI embedded in standalone web apps and business tools differs.

visual.alt: Two cards showing Firefly as a standalone web app and Firefly features in Adobe apps side by side.

states.label: Independent web app
states.body: Adobe Firefly is an independent web application used by firefly.adobe.com. Generative AI helps the creative flow of conceiving, creating, and communicating ideas. You can create images and videos with text descriptions, and if you don't like the results, you can edit the description and recreate it. To use, you must have a stable internet connection, an Adobe ID, follow the Generative AI user guidelines, and be in a country where Firefly is available. If you violate the terms and conditions, your access may be restricted.

states.label: Built-in business tools
states.body: The same Firefly model family is also featured within Adobe's flagship apps and Adobe Stock. The advantage is that you can call AI right in the middle of document or design work. However, to use this feature, you must have a licensed copy of Firefly-based features in the Creative Cloud app. If your plan includes access to Firefly, you can't turn it off, but you can choose not to use the feature. Terms of use are determined by the tool's terms and conditions, not by the stand-alone web app's description.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the types of tools, let's read the section about terms of use and disclosure in the document.

screens.title: Terms of Use section of the Firefly FAQ
screens.lead: Open each topic one by one to see what the FAQ says about terms of use, training data, and attribution information.

items.title: Can I use it commercially?
items.body: Work from features not marked as beta can be used in commercial projects. The output of beta features may also be used in commercial projects unless otherwise specified in the product. In other words, even within the same tool, you need to check whether the feature is beta or whether there are separate instructions for the product.

items.title: What did you learn with
items.body: He explains that the current Firefly creation model was trained on a dataset consisting of licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public domain content. To ensure they are commercially safe, we say we trained our initial commercial models on Adobe Stock images, publicly licensed content, and out-of-copyright public domain content.

items.title: Is my content also used for learning?
items.body: We state that we do not learn from Creative Cloud subscribers' personal content. Content from Adobe Stock contributors is included in the training data in accordance with the Contributor License Agreement. This description is specific to Adobe's tools; for other services, you should read their own documentation.

items.title: How do we indicate our use of AI?
items.body: Content Credentials are digital ingredient label-like devices that contain tamper-evident information such as production date, tools used, and editing history. It is based on an open technology standard called C2PA and can contain information indicating that generative AI has been used. Adobe notes that it automatically applies this information to some exports of Firefly output.

items.title: What happens to copyright?
items.body: Laws surrounding generative AI are changing rapidly in many countries, the FAQ explains, and advises people to contact legal experts in their region for discussions about copyright in generative output. Remember that the tool's FAQ won't decide this for you.

screens.outro: Now that you've read the conditions, let's summarize the items to check in the ad draft example.

screens.title: Explanation: When using generated images in advertising drafts
screens.lead: The instructor explains step by step the items to check before writing the created image in the new product advertisement draft. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: The background image for the new product advertisement design was created with Firefly. Since this draft will be published in external media, you should check all terms of use, rights of others, and disclosure methods.

steps.title: Step 1: Check the commercial use terms
steps.body: Check whether the feature that created the image was beta, and see if there are any conditions written separately for the product. The FAQ explains that the output of features not marked as beta can be used in commercial projects, and beta features can be used unless otherwise specified. Record the results of this check.

steps.title: Step 2: Read the description of training data and rights
steps.body: Read the sources of training data described by the tool. The explanation that learning was done with licensed content and public domain provides evidence that the tool was designed to be safe, but it does not guarantee that the results will always be problem-free.

steps.title: Step 3: Check the rights of others
steps.body: Check that images do not contain faces of real people, trademarks of other companies, or recognizable artwork. Regardless of the tool's terms of use, you cannot use images that infringe the rights of others.

steps.title: Step 4: Disclose in accordance with organizational regulations and media standards
steps.body: How to indicate the use of AI is governed by your organization's regulations and the standards of the medium in which the advertisement appears. It must not appear to be man-made with the intent to deceive. Where possible, maintain Content Credentials to verify the source.

steps.title: Step 5: Human review before final approval
steps.body: The person approving the draft looks at the image and verifies that the preceding items are noted. Only when someone is responsible can you respond when a problem arises.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: The result in this case is a check mark with five confirmation marks next to the draft. As easy as it is to make, it is important to check before writing briefly and regularly.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the checklist, let's finish with one habit.

screens.title: The habit of checking the terms of use of products
screens.lead: Let's organize what we've seen so far into one habit. Please read while thinking about the creations you have created.

paragraphs: Terms of use for generated images vary depending on the tool and feature. Even for the same tool, it may vary depending on whether the feature is in beta or whether there are separate instructions for the product, and AI built into a business tool follows the terms and conditions of that tool.

Sources of training data and terms of commercial use are stated in the tool's documentation. Reading the documentation is the quickest way to find out. However, in matters where the law changes quickly, such as copyright, documents cannot decide for you, so consult an expert.

The fact of AI use can be disclosed in accordance with organizational rules and circumstances, and source indication devices such as Content Credentials can be used. The important thing is not to deceive the reader. Finally, it is reviewed by a human before final use. If you record the confirmed conditions with the date, you can explain the basis to anyone who asks later. The more the material is exposed to the outside world, such as an advertisement, the more valuable the record becomes. A short note is sufficient for recording.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Just because something is easy to make doesn't mean it can be written off. Check the terms of use, rights of others, and disclosure arrangements before using them.

glossary.def: This is a generative AI function that creates new images with text descriptions, etc.
These are the usage rules set by the tool, such as whether the product can be used commercially.
Source information that includes production date, tools used, and editing history. Based on C2PA standards.
This is an AI function that is included in document or design apps and can be used right away while working.

misconceptions.myth: Images created by AI can be freely used anywhere.
misconceptions.fact: Conditions vary depending on the tool and function. You should check whether it is a beta and the conditions written on the product, and also check other people's rights separately.

misconceptions.myth: Disclosing your use of AI is always unnecessary.
misconceptions.fact: You may need to display it according to your organization's regulations and media standards. It must not appear to be man-made for the purpose of deception.

misconceptions.myth: Built-in AI has the same terms of use as regular web tools.
misconceptions.fact: Terms of use follow the terms and conditions set by each tool. Just because it's inside an app doesn't mean the description for a standalone web app applies.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Terms of use of the product are checked for each tool and feature.
Sources of training data and terms of commercial use are stated in the tool's documentation.
We disclose the use of AI in accordance with organizational rules and utilize attribution mechanisms.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What are the terms of use and disclosure of works I have created or will create?

checks.q: What is the best description of Content Credentials?
options: Information such as an ‘ingredient list’ containing production date, tools used, and editing history can contain the fact of AI use.
It is a device that automatically changes the copyright of an image to ownership.
This is a setting that excludes generated images from training data.
This is a license that allows commercial use of beta function results.
checks.explain: Content Credentials (C2PA standard) contain production history, including information that AI was used, and are automatically applied to some exports.

wrong.1: It is information that informs history and is not a device to transfer rights.
wrong.2: It is a separate concept from training data.
wrong.3: Commercial use is determined by the beta marking of the feature and the terms and conditions written on the product.

checks.intro: Find out for yourself what the attribution information you just saw means. Results are not recorded, and commentary appears immediately after you select an option.

checks.q: Before using the created image in the advertisement design, place it in the confirmation order.
items: Check whether the feature you used is beta or not and what the terms of commercial use are.
Read the sources and rights of training data explained by the tool
Check whether it infringes on other people's rights, such as face, trademark, or actual person.
AI use is flagged in compliance with organizational policies and final human review is conducted.
checks.explain: Confirm the terms of use and rights basis, check the rights of others, and finish with disclosure and final review.
checks.intro: Before writing the created image, think about the confirmation order and arrange it. Results are not recorded.
